AbstractText.Label: Objective
AbstractText.content: Few studies have examined relations between one important aspect of spiritual/religious functioning-spiritual distress-and pain-related outcomes, and none has examined how spiritual distress and depression conjointly relate to chronic pain. The goal of the present study, then, was to examine veterans' spiritual distress as a predictor of two aspects of chronic pain, catastrophizing and interference, testing a mediational model of depression.

AbstractText.Label: Design
AbstractText.content: Four hundred thirty-six patients seeking treatment in a chronic pain management clinic responded to a mailed survey assessing demographics, spiritual distress, depression, pain catastrophizing, and pain interference.

AbstractText.Label: Setting
AbstractText.content: Participants were drawn from a list of patients enrolled in a chronic pain rehabilitation program at a large Midwestern Veterans Affairs health care system.

AbstractText.Label: Subjects
AbstractText.content: Participants were 436 veterans seeking chronic pain rehabilitation. The sample was predominantly Caucasian and male.

AbstractText.Label: Methods
AbstractText.content: Survey data were subjected to mediational analysis, assessing both direct effects of spiritual distress on pain outcomes and indirect effects of spiritual distress through depression.

AbstractText.Label: Results
AbstractText.content: Results showed that spiritual distress was moderately strongly related to both pain outcomes. Further, depression mediated links between spiritual distress and pain catastrophizing (partially) and interference (fully).

AbstractText.Label: Conclusions
AbstractText.content: These results have implications for further research in spiritually integrated care as a component of holistic, integrative approaches to the management of chronic pain.
